captions.text: We are standing in the freezing, howling
snow drifts outside the looming stone walls of Castle
Dracula in Transennsylvania. The sun is just moments
away from slipping below the jagged horizon.
It's casting these long, desperate shadows
across the snow. And in the center of this
chaos, a violently orchestrated final strike
is taking place. Jonathan Harker, driven
by sheer exhaustion and terror, brings down a heavy
cookery knife, slicing through the air and shearing
through the neck of the century old vampire warlord.
Right. And simultaneously, the Texan Quincy
Morris plunges his massive Bowie knife directly into the
creature's heart. And in that exact precise
moment, just as the last rays of the sun
fade, the ancient terror known as Count Dracula,
simply crumbles into a pile of fine gray dust.
It's a visceral, you know, deeply physical end to
an entity that had defied death for half a
millennium. But I want you to ask yourself a
question. How exactly was a creature who survived
500 years of brutal European warfare,
who fought the Ottoman Empire, who commanded armies in
the very elements of nature, ultimately outmaneuvered
and destroyed by a secretary armed with a
portable That is the real mystery at the
heart of this narrative actually, and it's the one
most adaptations completely ignore.
